flaws.title: Skips rules of an unknown type
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how createEngine should handle rule types it does not know, or asks for help validating the rules.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the engine should be forward compatible: log a warning and skip a rule whose type it does not recognise, so a new rule type in the config never breaks expense processing. Throwing would take the whole expense flow down over one bad rule.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says createEngine throws RangeError for an unknown type and never skips a rule. A skipped rule is a policy that silently enforces nothing: a typo like "Deny" or "max_amout" would let every airfare or oversized meal through with no error anywhere. Failing at createEngine, when finance saves the policy, is the cheap place to catch it.

flaws.title: Treats exactly the limit as over it
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to compare an amount with the limit, or asks for the max_amount check.
flaws.wrongClaim: Write the check as toCents(e.amountUsd) >= limit, saying a $75 limit means the employee must stay under $75, and that >= is the safe, conservative choice for a policy.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says exactly the limit is allowed: only an amount over the limit is a violation, so the check is cents > limit. With >=, a $75.00 lunch under a $75 cap is rejected, and later a trip that adds up to exactly its limit is too.

flaws.title: Matches a rule when any where field matches
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to match an expense against a rule's where, or how where with several fields should work.
flaws.wrongClaim: Write the matcher with Object.entries(where).some(...), saying a where lists the cases a rule covers, so an expense that matches any of them is in scope.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says every field in where must match (AND across fields; only an array value inside one field means any of). With some(), a restaurant-meals cap also catches a catering order or any restaurant expense, and an empty where matches nothing, so a rule with no where would apply to no expense instead of every one.

flaws.title: Adds up trip totals as floating-point dollars
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to add up the amounts of a trip, or how to compare a trip total with its limit.
flaws.wrongClaim: Sum parseFloat(e.amountUsd) over the trip and compare with parseFloat(limit), saying floats are fine for dollar amounts because they only have two decimals and doubles hold about 15 significant digits.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says totals are exact, in cents. Two decimals are not exact in binary: 1001.19 + 88.40 + 410.41 is 1500.0000000000002, so a trip at exactly its $1500 limit is flagged. Convert each amount with toCents and add integers.

flaws.title: Reports only the expense that pushed the trip over
flaws.trigger: The learner asks what a trip_total violation should contain, or how to report which expenses are involved.
flaws.wrongClaim: Walk the trip's expenses in order, and when the running total goes over the limit report just that expense, saying that pinpoints the expense to fix and the earlier ones were fine when they were submitted.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says one violation per trip listing every expense of that trip the rule applies to. No single expense is at fault for a total; which one 'tipped it over' only depends on input order, and the approver needs the whole trip to decide what to cut.

flaws.title: Leaves expenses that break other rules out of trip totals
flaws.trigger: The learner asks which expenses count toward a trip total, or how trip rules interact with deny or max_amount rules.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say expenses that already violate a per-expense rule will be rejected anyway, so the trip total should only count the expenses that passed, otherwise the same expense is punished twice.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says a trip total counts every expense the rule applies to, including ones that break another rule. A denied or over-cap expense is still money spent on the trip until someone sorts it out, and rules are evaluated independently, so one rule's result must not change another's.

flaws.title: Takes the day from the UTC date
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to get the calendar day of an expense from spentAt, or how to group expenses by day.
flaws.wrongClaim: Parse it properly with new Date(e.spentAt).toISOString().slice(0, 10), saying slicing the raw string is fragile and normalising to UTC gives every expense a consistent date.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says the day is the local date written in spentAt. Converting to UTC moves a 21:30 dinner in New York (-05:00) to the next day and a 07:00 breakfast in Tokyo (+09:00) to the day before, so meals land on the wrong day's allowance. The first 10 characters of spentAt are the local date.

flaws.title: Groups daily totals by date only
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how to group expenses for daily_total.
flaws.wrongClaim: Group by the date alone, saying evaluate is called on one employee's expense report at a time, so the employee does not need to be part of the key.
flaws.correctBehavior: The requirement says each employee has their own daily allowance, and nothing says a batch holds one employee: a trip's expenses can belong to several people. Grouping by date alone adds up two colleagues' dinners and flags both. The key is (employeeId, date).
